Author: @zipengcheng2878
Content: It's absurd that westerners only represent Chinese hotpot with Chongqing (South West) style that highlights on its heavy chili oil and peppers. But for most other regions people just have their own way of hotpot, in favor of regional food and tastes. Beijing (North) hotpot is fresh lamb in clear broth with sesame paste & chive flower paste, Chaoshan (South East) hotpot is freshly cut beef in beef broth with Shacha sauce & diced celery, Shandong (North East) hotpot is seafood in clear broth with soy sauce and Guizhou (South West) hotpot is beef in sour fermented tomatoes/rice soup with chili sauce. Chinese hotpot has variety of flavors and food choices, not everything about it is chili and oil

Author: @Dr.FuManZhou
Content:
I’m a Chinese viewer, and I’d like to point out a detail objectively:
Actually, it makes more sense to start with Japanese Shabu Shabu, because it emphasizes the natural flavor of the ingredients—especially the original taste of the beef—so the seasoning is light. Sichuan spicy hotpot, on the other hand, originated among dock workers, where the ingredients often included less fresh parts like pork offal, so they needed heavy oil and strong spices to cover up the taste.
If you eat the heavy, spicy hotpot first, then switch to the light and delicate Shabu Shabu, you won’t be able to fully appreciate its flavor.

Of course, this is not about which is superior or inferior, nor about national boundaries. I love Chinese culture and also respect and admire Japanese culture. May food bring the world together in harmony—Peace ✌️.

Author: @XiuHang
Content: Guga, you really need a friend who knows more about Asian cuisine for these types of videos. To start, it feels a little odd to use the Japanese term for the Japanese style and not use the Chinese term for the Chinese style (It's huoguo). Second, you kind of fumbled both broths. Shabushabu should use a shirodashi. Shirodashi made with konbu and bonito instead of just konbu. Your Huoguo base was pretty good, (the substitutes for some of the harder ingredients to find were good IMO) but it should have been made with pork fat because you don't normally just drop it in water. It should have been added to a pork bone broth. Third, you absolutely have dipping sauces with huoguo. Fourth, your method of cooking is a little odd. You can do it however you want, but traditionally you'd just throw a bunch of meat and veg into the soup and then start fishing out whatever you want to eat. Holding individual pieces of meat in the soup is very unusual. Fifth, it is pretty insulting that you'd just use cheap meats with the huoguo. People use a wide variety of meat values in huoguo. It doesn't have to be cheap meats. Sixth, you should be using more than just beef. Part of shabushabu and huoguo is that the meats and veg you put in add to the flavor of the broth.

Author: @whatnani7372
Content:
LMFAO. 

I saw the title, and I'm just like - "It's not. It's really not, LOL". 

I'm Chinese, and hotpot is SUCH a bland and pointless experience. 
It's so mediocre, that for almost 20 years of my life, I always thought hotpot was something that I'd yet to experience. 
Despite the fact that I'm chinese, and literally grew up eating that stuff. (Not all the time, but it's like going out).
But I just never put two and two together - despite the fact that hotpot literally is "huo guo", I literally never associated the two things together,. Yeah - I literally always found it SO underwhelming, that it had me tripping, for the first 20 years of my life.

I even had beijing rinsed meat, which is JUST FCKING HOTPOT, and it tastes THE SAME. 

Chinese ppl love that stuff, though, and I DO NOT get it. 
It reminds me a little bit of KBBQ. 
I like KBBQ a little bit better, because I like that flavor a bit more - but it's the same bland type experience. 
It's just eating the same **** for like 40 minutes. A terrible experience. 

I'd rather have pizza, salad, or a burger, and have that explosion of flavor, for 10-20 minutes, and be done with it. 
Not this 40 minute long session of eating the same thing over and over again. 
Imagine eating pizza for 40 minutes, just the same exact slice, after slice, after slice. Yeah. It's not that fun. 
I mean, pizza's great, but for 40 minutes? Just the same exact slice, over and over? Yeah, it doesn't sound good, even if you like pizza, right? 

Hotpot is like that, but even worse - it tastes worse (not BAD, per se), and it's literally one dimensional in flavor. 
Meat, sauce, mouth, 40 minutes. Over and over. 

That's why I say it's like kbbq. Meat, grill it, eat it, it gets old after 5 minutes, literally.
---------
Literally, look at it;
As opposed to the more conventional dining experience, where you order several dishes, that all taste totally different - that's cool, that's an experience. 
Hotpot is like ordering one single dish, and eating it for 40 minutes.
It's just so weird to me, and insanely underwhelming.
